{"id": "15:29/q07", "question": "What is the nature of the spirit referred to here?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over bodily substance, immaterial substance, life as an accident, heart temperament, transcendent command, and divine power; several also acknowledge limited knowledge of its nature.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q07/p1", "position": "It is a created subtle body that gives life and persists apart from the changing visible body.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Baghawī define it as life-giving subtle body; Qurṭubī cites reports and identifies nafs and rūḥ as names for one referent. Ālūsī attributes this to the Sunni majority and Juwaynī; Laqqānī calls it luminous, self-living and imperishable, permeating organs like rosewater; verificationists compare oil in sesame, with persistent particles outlasting bodily change. Al-Jalāl says proofs of selfhood beyond the visible frame do not exclude a subtle body; Ālūsī says its special divine property prevents a regress of spirits."}, {"id": "15:29/q07/p2", "position": "It is an immaterial, self-subsisting substance, distinct from the body and bodily accidents.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Ghazālī and verificationists: universal intelligibles cannot inhere in indivisible or divisible matter; the Shaykh cites direct self-awareness; Plato cites imagined vast nonexistent forms; further arguments cite unified perception, organ awareness and continuity of personal identity as the frame changes. The author of al-Hayākil notes awareness of self when bodily parts are forgotten; Ālūsī defends the possibility of distinct spaceless creatures and says only God's independence is unique. Al-Jalāl replies that these proofs may establish only distinction from the visible frame."}, {"id": "15:29/q07/p3", "position": "The spirit is life itself, an accident inhering in the body.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports identification with life; Ālūsī reports a visible-frame account, a later argument from it against servants creating acts, and al-Qāḍī's attribution to most theologians and Ustādh Abū Isḥāq. The Imam objects that the person persists while bodily parts change; this account raises the accident-in-an-accident problem."}, {"id": "15:29/q07/p4", "position": "The spirit is the balanced temperament of the heart's blood.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this as a further account."}, {"id": "15:29/q07/p5", "position": "It is a real transcendent divine-command being, the person's essential self rather than a physical function.", "reasons": "Elmalılı links the bestowed spirit to 17:85; Kūran Yolu says 17:85 leaves its nature little known yet affirms a real metaphysical being linking humans to the divine realm, and makes spirit the true self. Ghazālī calls it divine reality; Study Quran reports commentators who take al-rūḥ more literally. Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes its self-existence and independence at death; Ibn al-Jawzī and Ālūsī stress limits of knowledge."}, {"id": "15:29/q07/p6", "position": "It is God's power or a specially chosen created spirit from His power.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the power interpretation; Abū ʿAbd Allāh and Samāʿa say spirit comes from God's power or malakūt without diminishing Him; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it active power emanating from essential power. Abū Jaʿfar calls it a specially chosen created spirit, favored above other spirits, from which Adam was breathed."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q08", "question": "Are human souls all of one species?", "turns_on": "Whether shared faculties establish one essence, or persistent personal and prophetic differences imply distinct soul kinds.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q08/p1", "position": "Human souls share one species.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Ghazālī and the Shaykh, but says the Shaykh supplies no proof. Advocates argue that essential difference would make souls composite and bodily, that all people share capacities for knowledge and moral traits, and that all self-knowing immaterial selves apprehend the same cognitive and volitional essence. Ālūsī replies that composition need not imply body, induction of equal capacities is inadequate, and the self-knowledge argument would assimilate all separate beings."}, {"id": "15:29/q08/p2", "position": "Souls may differ in species.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports a small group and the author of al-Muʿtabar, who cites differences in knowledge, strength, anger, restraint and prophetic power despite similar temperaments. Ālūsī regards this as weak persuasion, while his critiques leave common species unproved."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q09", "question": "Did individual human souls exist before their bodies?", "turns_on": "How souls become distinct, whether origination requires bodily matter, and how reports of prior spirits or everlasting souls are understood.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q09/p1", "position": "They originate when particular bodies become fit to receive them.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Ghazālī, Aristotle and followers, comparing the soul to an image appearing in a polished mirror. Ghazālī argues one preexistent soul cannot divide and already multiple souls lack individuating matter or attributes; Ālūsī further grounds individuality in bodily attachment and persisting self-awareness. He answers division, accidental distinction and transmigration objections, yet records objections about circular or infinite differentiation, essential differences, earlier bodies and endless accidents; he calls al-Muʿtabar's memory argument weak."}, {"id": "15:29/q09/p2", "position": "Souls preexist bodies, or are eternal.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports the ungraded two-thousand-years-prior spirits report and the ancient philosophers' arguments: origination would require matter, infinite prior bodies would yield impossible infinite surviving souls, and originated things could not be everlasting. Ghazālī instead reads the report as angels preceding cosmic bodies; Ālūsī rejects the inferences from matter, infinity and everlastingness."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q10", "question": "What do reports of Muhammad's being a prophet before Adam's completion mean?", "turns_on": "Whether 'first' means temporal existence or priority in divine plan.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q10/p1", "position": "They say Muhammad was first in creation and already a prophet while Adam was between water and clay.", "reasons": "Ālūsī cites two Prophetic sayings."}, {"id": "15:29/q10/p2", "position": "They refer to divine decree and intended purpose, not Muhammad's actual prior bodily existence.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports an architectural analogy: the final house is first in design; God's plan and the Preserved Tablet precede realization. Human creation aims at nearness through prophecy, completed in Muhammad, the final historical prophet and purest descendant of Adam. The Pen and Tablet can be understood as spiritual teacher and learner; 96:4 supports the analogy."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q11", "question": "Why is the spirit called رُّوحِى, 'My spirit'?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive chiefly marks ownership and honor, immediate creation, likeness in certain qualities, or power as the spirit's source.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q11/p1", "position": "It is God's created possession, singled out for honor and distinction.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī explain an honorific ownership genitive; Qurṭubī compares God's house, camel, earth, sky and month and links 4:171, as does Bayḍāwī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls rūḥ a generic class term; Abū Jaʿfar compares God's attributed created image to the Kaʿba; Abū Ḥayyān adds direct creation and placement."}, {"id": "15:29/q11/p2", "position": "The attribution marks direct divine creation without an intermediary and special nearness.", "reasons": "Bursevī says God personally shaped Adam and breathed, linking the divine breath to knowledge of all gracious and majestic Names and to the 'shadow' of 25:45; al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya relates special rank to 50:16. Ghazālī says no intermediate origin or matter was used and also allows honorific attribution; Abū Ḥayyān likewise mentions direct creation."}, {"id": "15:29/q11/p3", "position": "The spirit's likeness to divine qualities or its origin in divine power explains the attribution.", "reasons": "Ghazālī compares sunlight from the sun and cites spacelessness and universal knowledge while distinguishing degrees; Ālūsī says creaturely dependence preserves God's uniqueness. Ṭabāṭabāʾī's reports derive spirit from God's power without treating it as a lost divine part; Study Quran reports a power reading."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q12", "question": "Why is the divine act phrased in the singular here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q12/p1", "position": "Adam's spirit was breathed directly after his creation, whereas Mary's conception through Gabriel uses the plural of majesty.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī makes the contrast."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q13", "question": "What does the فَ in فَقَعُوا۟ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q13/p1", "position": "It links the command to the 'when' condition, marking immediate succession after formation and breathing.", "reasons": "Rāzī emphasizes no intervening delay; Nasafī calls the imperative the answer to idhā and infers that a command can precede its execution. {"id": "15:29/q16", "question": "To whom was the angels' prostration directed?", "turns_on": "Whether 'to him' makes Adam the honored recipient of prostration or its direction while God remains the object of worship.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q16/p1", "position": "It was directed to Adam as a greeting and honor, while worship remained God's alone.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, al-Kalbī, Wāḥidī, Abū al-Qāsim, Baghawī and Qurṭubī distinguish greeting from worship; Wāḥidī and Study Quran compare Joseph's family in 12:100 and his dream in 12:4. {"id": "15:29/q17", "question": "Which angels were commanded to prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether this general command includes the highest angels in light of 7:206.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q17/p1", "position": "The command may include all heavenly angels.", "reasons": "Rāzī records this as one scope allowed by the general wording."}, {"id": "15:29/q17/p2", "position": "The command may include only some angels or the angels of earth, excluding those nearest God.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the narrower scopes and an argument from 7:206 that the nearest angels prostrate to God alone; he says that specific statement takes priority over this verse's general wording."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q18", "question": "What happened when angels were commanded to prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrated refusal involved earlier groups of angels as well as Iblīs.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q18/p1", "position": "Successive angelic groups refused and were burned, then another group obeyed while Iblīs remained among the first unbelievers.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās; Ibn ʿAṭiyya repeats Ṭabarī's report, saying another group was created and obeyed except Iblīs."}, {"id": "15:29/q18/p2", "position": "The angels obeyed, but Iblīs refused because he judged Adam by clay against his own fire.", "reasons": "Kūran Yolu says Iblīs preferred limited reasoning over God's command, missed Adam's spiritual origin and was cursed until Resurrection; Study Quran also says he overlooked the Hands, Spirit and knowledge by focusing on material origin."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q19", "question": "Why was Adam worthy of the angels' prostration?", "turns_on": "Whether the prostration indicates Adam's superior station or a trial of angels considered superior.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q19/p1", "position": "His perfected form, spirit, knowledge and divinely granted qualities made him worthy of honor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says worth lies in qualities and effects rather than material or conventional purity; Elmalılı and Iṣlāḥī tie elevation to spirit and perfected ability; Kūran Yolu ties rank to a transcendent spirit explained to angels by 2:30,33. Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya adds perfected form and knowledge; Study Quran reports the interpretation that humans stood above angels before the fall. Sulamī's inward reports add repentance, names and nearness."}, {"id": "15:29/q19/p2", "position": "The command tested superior angels, giving them an opportunity for great reward.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports al-Qaffāl's Muʿtazilite account, which maintains angelic superiority over Adam."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q20", "question": "What inward meaning is found in Adam's preparation and the angels' submission?", "turns_on": "The reports variously focus on Adam's disclosed qualities, the human duty to preserve them, and the perfected person's symbolic station.", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q20/p1", "position": "Adam's spirit receives special divine nearness, knowledge and will, so angelic dispute yields to submission.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān names spirit and repentance; al-Wāsiṭī says the spirit's knowledge and will depend on God's knowing and willing, its own action and speech are effaced, and its formed, attributed state brings it near. Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says the spirit descends through angels, jinn, devils and animals, gathering their qualities before joining Adam's specially prepared form."}, {"id": "15:29/q20/p2", "position": "The divine spark enables ascent and connection with God when preserved, and spiritual darkness when squandered.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī links the perfected abilities and divine spark to the angelic honor and says neglect makes a human worse than an animal."}, {"id": "15:29/q20/p3", "position": "The perfected person's prayer can mirror both sides of Adam's prostration at an inward level.", "reasons": "Bursevī interprets a perfected shaykh's funeral prayer as the spirit both prostrating and being prostrated to, while the outward legal prayer remains supplication."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q21", "question": "Does intellect and faith persist after bodily death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q21/p1", "position": "Intellect, perception, faith and sainthood belong to the spirit and persist after death.", "reasons": "Bursevī recounts a dream in which his shaykh performed ablution after death, ascended, returned for his own funeral and affirmed continuing earthly intellect and perception; Bursevī infers these spiritual qualities do not change."}]}
{"id": "15:29/q22", "question": "What rule about washing the deceased does Bursevī draw?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q22/p1", "position": "The deceased should be washed because death agony ends ablution; even a perfected believer follows the outward rule.", "reasons": "Bursevī says the complete believer remains pure since ritual hadath is not impurity, yet outwardly lacks ablution and is washed like an imperfect person."}]}

{"id": "15:29/q25", "question": "How does this verse relate to other Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:29/q25/p1", "position": "It repeats and echoes other creation and prostration accounts.", "reasons": "Study Quran says it repeats 38:72, compares 32:9, and cites 2:34, 7:11, 17:61, 18:50, 20:116 and 38:73–74; it also compares Joseph's family's bowing in 12:100 with his dream in 12:4. {"id": "16:17/q06", "question": "What does the interrogative fa add to the comparison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:17/q06/p1", "position": "It directs denial at an imagined inference of likeness from God's preceding mighty acts.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi explains the fa after the interrogative hamza in this way."}]}
{"id": "16:17/q07", "question": "Why does the comparison put the Creator before the noncreator?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:17/q07/p1", "position": "The reversal exposes idolaters' act of lowering God to the level of powerless creatures by equating them in worship.", "reasons": "Al-Razi frames the objection that the comparison might be reversed; al-Zamakhshari, reported by Abu Hayyan and al-Samin, answers through their equation in naming and worship. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Burhan, al-Biqa'i and al-Itqan stress the sharper rebuke gained by lowering the higher party; al-Burhan says it confronts the idolaters on their own terms. Al-Alusi adds that possession properly precedes absence."}]}
{"id": "16:17/q08", "question": "What does the comparison establish about God and worship?", "turns_on": "The latter notes add implications about accountability or divine choice; they do not contest the denial of equality.", "positions": [{"id": "16:17/q08/p1", "position": "Creator and noncreator cannot be equal; worship and divinity belong to the Creator alone.", "reasons": "Muqatil names the four idols. Al-Thalabi and al-Qurtubi cite 31:11 and 46:4 or 35:40 as challenges to show another's creation. Al-Wahidi's exegetes compare gratitude owed to a benefactor with that owed to a nonbenefactor. Yahya, Jishumi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Qatada add idols' inability to benefit or harm; Yahya also denies their power over resurrection and glosses al-nushur as resurrection; al-Razi adds their lack of awareness, power and choice. Al-Biqa'i invokes God's knowledge, wisdom, power, free choice and universal benefits. Ibn Ashur says the question repudiates the polytheists' partnership claim; al-Tabataba'i says created existence and effects belong to God. Asad and others stress reflection on the contrast."}, {"id": "16:17/q08/p2", "position": "The verse also directs readers to monotheism and accountability in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Islahi names both implications without developing a separate argument in this note."}, {"id": "16:17/q08/p3", "position": "Differences among created things show that God acts by choice and can bring about whatever He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i argues that differences in existence and qualities have no explanation except choice."}]}
{"id": "16:17/q09", "question": "Does the creation argument settle whether humans create their own acts?", "turns_on": "Whether any act of creation would imply divinity, or the verse concerns God's cosmic creation and the idols' incapacity while allowing limited human agency.", "positions": [{"id": "16:17/q09/p1", "position": "Yes; creation belongs uniquely to God, so human acts are created by Him, not by their human doers.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi's associates say a person creating his acts would partner God in origination.
